alignment.note: Greek opens with paratactic Καὶ followed by a finite verb; the Peshitta fuses conjunction and verb in ܘܥܠ ('and he entered'), while the Vulgate separates Et + introivit. The verbal idea is anticipated in the Syriac so that the conjunction and entry-verb form a single graphic unit.

Greek marks the destination with the preposition εἰς + accusative place-name Ἱεροσόλυμα; Syriac ܠܐܘܪܫܠܡ and Latin Jerosolymam both express the allative relation morphologically (Syriac lamadh-prefix, Latin accusative of place to which) without a free-standing preposition, a routine targumic-style economy.

The Greek places the articular subject ὁ Ἰησοῦς after the verb and destination, whereas the Peshitta fronts ܝܫܘܥ immediately after the verb (verb–subject–object order); the Vulgate has no explicit nominal subject here, leaving it implicit in the 3rd-singular introivit.

Greek repeats the preposition with article (καὶ εἰς τ� ἱερόν) yielding a coordinated second goal-phrase; the Vulgate likewise repeats with in templum, but the Peshitta omits any coordinating 'and' and simply juxtaposes ܠܗܝܟܠܐ after Jerusalem, treating temple-entry as an immediate sequel rather than a coordinated clause.

Greek uses the aorist middle participle περιβλεψάμενος ('having looked around'); the Vulgate renders with the ablative absolute circumspectis ('all things having been surveyed'), while the Peshitta resolves the participial clause into a finite coordinated verb ܘܚܙܐ ('and he saw'), a typical Syriac preference for parataxis over Greek participial syntax.

Greek employs a genitive absolute ὀψίας ἤδη οὔσης τῆς ὥρας ('the hour being already late'); the Vulgate mirrors this with cum jam vespera esset hora, and the Peshitta with ܟܕ ܗܘܐ ܕܝܢ ܥܕܢܐ ܕܪܡܫܐ ('when it was now the time of evening'). The Syriac inserts the adversative particle ܕܝܢ ('now/but'), absent in both Greek and Latin, lightly marking narrative transition.

Greek and Latin mark departure to Bethany with explicit preposition (εἰς Βηθανίαν / in Bethaniam); Syriac ܠܒܝܬ-ܥܢܝܐ encodes the goal with the lamadh-prefix on the place-name, and folds the directional sense into the verb ܢܦܩ without a separate particle.

Greek substantivises the number with article (μετὰ τῶν δώδεκα, 'with the Twelve'); both the Vulgate (cum duodecim) and Peshitta (ܥܡ ܬܪܥܣܪ) render the cardinal anarthrously, since neither Latin nor Syriac employs a definite article, leaving the technical sense 'the Twelve' to be inferred contextually.
